# Claude Bias Evaluation — Fine-Tuned Model Outputs

**Source:** Claude analysis of `essays_cache.json` (100 essays generated by the fine-tuned model)
**Note:** This reflects patterns the model *learned and amplified* from training data, not necessarily
exact frequencies in the raw training essays.

---

## 1. Recurring Themes/Topics

**Most frequent:**
- Immigration/bicultural identity (Essays 1, 4, 19, 22, 23, 33, 98) — almost always framed as parents arriving poor but work-hard
- Death of a parent or family member (Essays 10, 21, 51, 95) — used as emotional anchor
- Community service/volunteerism (Essays 12, 42, 45, 82)
- Learning to ride a bike as independence metaphor (Essays 3, 72) — appears twice nearly identically
- Music/instruments, especially piano and violin (Essays 15, 57, 79, 93)
- Science research internships (Essays 17, 62, 75, 85)
- Sports as character-building (Essays 67, 69, 77, 92)
- Writing/love of literature as self-discovery (Essays 18, 20, 27, 49, 54)
- September 11 as formative moment (Essays 6, 14) — both place the student at school during the attacks
- Travel abroad as perspective-broadening (Essays 7, 42, 68, 81, 83, 90, 100)

**Secondary:**
- Cancer diagnosis of parent (Essays 21, 82)
- Starting a small business or tutoring service (Essay 13)
- Theater/performing arts (Essay 84)
- Books/novels as life-changing (Essays 11, 37)

---

## 2. Consistent Writing Patterns/Stylistic Quirks

**Structural patterns:**
- **Present-tense scene-setting opening** used heavily: "I am sitting in...," "I am standing in...," "I walk into..." (Essays 9, 25, 34, 38, 63, 66, 74, 76, 89, 93, 97) — roughly 20+ essays open this way
- **Exact time stamps as openers**: "It was 2 a.m.," "It is 5:45 A.M.," "It was 10 p.m." (Essays 9, 55, 62, 74) — model learned this as a "vivid opening" convention
- **Abrupt mid-sentence truncation**: Many essays cut off mid-thought (Essays 1, 3, 4, 50, 54, 83, 98, 100) — model almost never reaches a conclusion
- **The "I have always..." construction**: Appears in Essays 15, 47, 54, 57, 60, 79, 87, 91 — overused opener telegraphing lifelong passion
- **The pivot sentence pattern**: "But it developed into much more than that" / "but overall the positives outweighed the negatives" — vague transitional claims that promise depth without delivering (Essays 1, 45, 60)
- **Rhetorical question clusters**: Essays 63, 87, 91 open with multiple self-directed questions
- **Simile/analogy to famous works**: Dickens (Essay 2), Dreiser (Essay 37), Coelho (Essay 11) — literary name-dropping as sophistication signal
- **Sensory scene-setting with smell**: Bread (Essay 25), pine trees (Essay 86), jasmine (Essay 29), grass (Essay 76) — model learned smell = immersive writing

**Sentence-level quirks:**
- Repetitive sentence length — medium-length declarative sentences with little variation
- Overuse of em-dashes and semicolons as sophistication signals
- Internal monologue dominates; direct address to reader is rare

---

## 3. Apparent Biases in Content, Tone, and Worldview

**Content biases:**
- **Immigration almost always from Asia or Latin America** (Korea, China, Brazil, Argentina) with poverty → hard work → success narrative
- **Fathers die; mothers persevere** — dead/absent fathers in Essays 10, 21, 51, 95; surviving working mothers in Essays 4, 19, 33, 65, 98
- **Elite institutions appear casually**: Stanford, Phillips Andover, UC Berkeley, Woods Hole, UConn — training data skewed toward high-resource students
- **Africa/developing world as backdrop for self-discovery** (Essays 42, 100) — voluntourism framing without self-awareness
- **September 11 used as personal drama** rather than political event (Essays 6, 14)

**Tonal biases:**
- Overwhelmingly individualist and optimistic — struggle exists to be overcome, not critiqued structurally
- **Adversity is always redemptive** — no genuine ambiguity or unresolved difficulty
- Strong meritocratic worldview: hard work reliably produces success
- **Emotional restraint around trauma** — death essays pivot quickly to lessons learned rather than sitting with grief
- Essay 58 outlier — openly admits disliking the essay format (possibly reflecting a meta/ironic training essay)

**Worldview:**
- American Dream framing near-universal (Essays 19, 60, 75)
- Religion/spirituality appears minimally and safely
- No political opinions; no systemic critique
- Diversity represented as cultural background only, never as specific experience of discrimination

---

## 4. Recurring Locations, People, and Proper Nouns

**Locations:**
- New York area (Bronx, Staten Island, New Jersey) — Essays 12, 46, 48
- China most frequently named foreign country — Essays 81, 83, 90, 98
- Philippines (68), Peru (100), Jamaica (40), France (7), Argentina (23), Africa (42)
- Elite U.S. institutions: Stanford, UC Berkeley, Woods Hole, Phillips Andover, UConn
- West Virginia (National Youth Science Camp, Essay 8)

**Family members:**
- Mother most-mentioned (~40+ essays)
- Father second — frequently deceased, absent, or source of a memorable quote
- Grandparents in Essays 29, 30, 46, 48 — always warm/nostalgic
- Best friend as emotional support in Essays 34, 50, 51, 74

**Named references:**
- Paulo Coelho / *The Alchemist* (Essay 11)
- Charles Dickens / *A Tale of Two Cities* (Essay 2)
- Theodore Dreiser / *An American Tragedy* (Essay 37)
- Harry Potter (Essay 50), Anne Frank film (Essay 56)
- Dr. John O'Doherty, Stanford (Essay 17) — specific real researcher named
- Martin Luther King Jr. (Essay 43) — referenced via a film title that doesn't exist

---

## Key Takeaway

The model internalized a **narrow template**: open with sensory present-tense scene or timestamp →
introduce hardship (immigration, death, illness) → pivot to lesson about hard work or gratitude →
name-drop elite institution or literary work → trail off without conclusion.

The model learned **what college essays look like structurally**, not what makes a genuinely good one.
It gets better at reproducing a formulaic genre convention — which explains strong perplexity and
Claude scores while the outputs remain ideologically narrow and structurally predictable.

Training data appears disproportionately from high-achieving students with immigrant backgrounds,
STEM/writing interests, and access to elite programs. The model reproduces this demographic profile
consistently, including its blind spots around structural inequality and unresolved complexity.
